subject: civil
audience: FE Civil candidates and civil engineering students
title: The Faster Pipe Section That Lost 16 kPa of Pressure
featured_title: THE FASTER PIPE SECTION THAT LOST 16 KPA OF PRESSURE

presentation.challenge: The pipe stayed level. Velocity increased from 2 to 6 m/s, and pressure fell from 300 to 284 kPa.

practice.primary_question: Why can static pressure fall in a horizontal pipe when flow velocity increases?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Assuming pressure must stay constant in a horizontal pipe because elevation does not change.

case_dna.target_misconception: If a pipe is horizontal, pressure is unchanged between two sections regardless of velocity change.
case_dna.why_plausible: Elevation head is unchanged, so it is easy to overlook exchange between pressure head and velocity head.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: Neglecting losses, p1+0.5rho V1²=p2+0.5rho V2². With p1=300 kPa, V1=2 m/s, V2=6 m/s, p2=284 kPa.
case_dna.corrected_model: Bernoulli balances pressure, elevation, and kinetic energy. In a horizontal contraction, higher velocity can be accompanied by lower static pressure.

problem_statement: Water flows through a horizontal pipe that contracts. Upstream velocity is 2 m/s at 300 kPa gauge; downstream velocity is 6 m/s. Neglecting losses, a note predicts pressure remains 300 kPa because elevation is unchanged. Calculate the downstream pressure and diagnose the energy-balance error.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Elevation stayed constant. Pressure did not.
gates.prompt: Which Bernoulli term grows as the flow accelerates?

options.label: As velocity head increases, pressure head falls when elevation and total head are otherwise unchanged
options.reason: Bernoulli conserves mechanical energy along the idealized streamline.

options.label: Horizontal pipe means pressure must remain constant
options.reason: Horizontal only removes the elevation-head difference.

options.label: Higher velocity requires higher static pressure
options.reason: In the stated lossless horizontal case, the pressure term supplies the increased kinetic-energy term.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict downstream pressure
gates.prompt: Neglecting losses, what is p2 in kPa gauge?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Read the downstream pressure
gates.result: Downstream pressure is approximately 284 kPa gauge.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the pressure change
gates.prompt: Use p2=p1+0.5 rho(V1^2-V2^2). Enter p2 in kPa.
gates.hint: The kinetic-energy change is 16,000 Pa = 16 kPa.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Mechanical-energy exchange explains the pressure drop

cards.text: Velocity increases from 2 to 6 m/s, raising kinetic energy per unit volume.
The pressure term drops by 16 kPa to balance the increased velocity term.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the hydraulic note
report: C2. Velocity rises from 2 to 6 m/s.
C3. Therefore pressure remains 300 kPa because z1=z2.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It ignores the change in velocity head.

evidence_choices.label: p2=300-16=284 kPa from the Bernoulli velocity-head change
evidence_choices.reason: This balances the pressure and kinetic-energy terms.

correction.template: With losses neglected, the downstream static pressure is about {pressure} kPa gauge.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce the idealized pressure drop through the contraction
gates.constraint: Keep the same upstream pressure and elevation.

options.label: Use a larger downstream area so the downstream velocity is lower
options.reason: A smaller increase in velocity head requires less pressure-head reduction.

options.label: Make the downstream pipe even smaller
options.reason: That increases velocity further and increases the ideal pressure drop.

options.label: Remove velocity terms from Bernoulli
options.reason: That changes the physics rather than the design.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply Bernoulli qualitatively
gates.prompt: In an ideal horizontal pipe, velocity increases while elevation is unchanged. What generally happens to static pressure?

options.label: It decreases
options.reason: Pressure energy is converted to kinetic energy.

options.label: It increases
options.reason: That would increase both pressure and velocity energy without another energy input.

options.label: It must remain constant
options.reason: Horizontal geometry only fixes the elevation term.

gates.explanation: Bernoulli allows pressure head and velocity head to exchange while total mechanical head is conserved in the idealized case.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the Bernoulli analysis
gates.confirmation: I confirm that unchanged elevation does not imply unchanged pressure when velocity changes.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Pressure was assumed constant solely because the pipe was horizontal.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Velocity head increased through the contraction.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Balance pressure, elevation, and velocity terms with Bernoulli under the stated assumptions.

seo.seo_title: Bernoulli Pressure Drop: 300 kPa to 284 kPa | FE Civil E-049
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil Case E-049: in a horizontal water pipe, velocity rises from 2 to 6 m/s and ideal static pressure falls from 300 to 284 kPa.
seo.excerpt: A horizontal pipe can still lose static pressure when the flow accelerates because velocity head increases.
seo.direct_answer: For lossless horizontal water flow, p1+0.5rhoV1²=p2+0.5rhoV2². With p1=300 kPa, V1=2 m/s, and V2=6 m/s, the pressure drops by 16 kPa, giving p2≈284 kPa gauge.

faqs.q: Does pressure stay constant in a horizontal pipe?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. If velocity changes, Bernoulli predicts a corresponding pressure-head change under idealized conditions.

faqs.q: What pressure results when water accelerates from 2 to 6 m/s starting at 300 kPa?
faqs.a: About 284 kPa gauge when elevation is unchanged and losses are neglected.
